newsitem.title: USA: Stephanopoulos likely to quit after U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Stephanopoulos likely to quit after U.S. election.

text.p: George Stephanopoulos, one of President Bill Clinton's top aides, was "running on nerves" and likely to quit along with other key administration figures if Clinton wins a second term, the New Yorker Magazine said on Sunday.

In a profile of the president's special adviser in its new issue by Pulitizer Prize winner David Remnick, the magazine says Stephanopoulos "will probably join a long list of administration officials ... who will be leaving sometime around Inauguration Day."

Among those mentioned by Remnick as likely not to serve in a Clinton second term are Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Defence Secretary William Perry, Attorney General Janet Reno and White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta.

In the profile called "Curious George," the 35-year-old Stephanopoulos says he was seriously considering leaving the White House. "I don't know what I will do. I've had a great run, a great ride, but it feels like I am done. It's not that I'm above it, but I can't do it anymore," he said.
Remnick said, "By now, Stephanopoulos is a burnt-out case ... he has become almost spectral; running on nerves, jumbo cups of black coffee and the desire to win one more time."

He said that after the debacle of the 1994 elections, in which the Democrats lost control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years, there were calls for Stephanopoulos' resignation. At that point, Clinton brought in Dick Morris, the political consultant who helped reposition the president in the centre of the political spectrum.

Morris, who resigned from the campaign in August after a tabloid newspaper revealed he had had a year-long affair with a prostitute, told the magazine he tried to improve the relationship between Clinton and Stephanopoulos, but the presidential aide said that was not true.
"Dick was constantly trying to get me fired, telling Clinton I was disloyal, that I was to blame for all our problems, making things up. There was a constant drumbeat."

Eventually the two men learned to work with each other and Stephanopoulos said his first reaction to Morris' resignation was to feel bad for him. But he said he changed his mind when he read how Morris had behaved.
"He betrayed the president so badly," he told the New Yorker.
